newsitem.title: USA: S. Korea foreign minister to visit United States.
newsitem.headline: S. Korea foreign minister to visit United States.

text.p: South Korea and the United States, whose joint Korean peace initiative is foundering, will focus on the issue when Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha visits Washington next week, the State Department said on Wednesday.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns said Yoo's official visit, at the invitation of Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, will take place May 22-24 and focus on all developments relating to the Korean peninsula, venue for the world's most heavily fortified border.
This includes the food crisis in North Korea, the U.S.-South Korean proposal for peace talks with Pyongyang and the 1994 U.S.-North Korean nuclear agreement, Burns said.
The meeting comes as diplomatic activity between North Korea on the one hand and the United States and South Korea on the other has turned disappointing.
"It's not a situation where things have broken off (but) we haven't made the the kind of progress that we'd like to make," one U.S. official said.

Despite some promising noises last month, North Korea still has not agreed to the peace talks proposal while the United States, South Korea and Japan have refused to consider large-scale food aid until Pyongyang enters into peace talks.
In addition, there has been no movement on two bilateral issues on which Washington insists there must be progress before there can be improved relations with Pyongyang.
For one thing North Korea has not rescheduled talks with the United States -- postponed by Pyongyang from this week -- on the North's sale of missiles and related technology to Iran, Syria and Libya.
For another, extensive U.S.-North Korean talks last week on the cases of 8,000 American servicemen missing from the 1950-53 Korean War produced no agreement.
Burns, asked whether the United States had received any recent response from North Korea on the peace talks proposal, described Pyongyang's reaction as "silence."
He said he could not explain why North Korea -- an "opaque" and isolated society -- was acting as it was. "The ball is in their court," he said.

The United States and South Korea in 1996 put forward the peace talks proposal, which aimed to defuse tensions on the Korean peninsula by replacing a fraying armistice with a formal peace treaty officially ending the Korean War. It would involve China as well as the United States and both Koreas.

North Korea told U.S. and South Korean negotiators in New York last month it would enter the peace talks but conditioned participation on large-scale food aid, the lifting of U.S. trade sanctions and on diplomatic recognition.

The U.N. World Food Programme, which says North Korea needs 1.3 million tons of food to meet its 1997 requirements, appealed for 200,000 tons of food worth $95.5 million, but received only $38 million, $25 million from the United States.

Although Washington has been willing to give small amounts of humanitarian aid, it refused to provide the kind of large-scale assistance that relief groups say is essential until the peace talks open.

South Korea, which donated $6 million to the recent WFP appeal, also holds that large-scale aid must await the peace talks. Japan decided to withhold all aid until Tokyo-Pyongyang ties were normalised and other issues put to rest, especially charges North Korea kidnapped a Japanese schoolgirl in 1977 and spirited her away to Pyongyang.

U.N. relief officials who returned from North Korea said Wednesday the country desperately needed food and reported severe malnutrition among children. The comments were part of a recent drumbeat by relief workers and U.S. officials said they expect the WFP to soon make another formal world appeal.
